title: Loyalty Points API
summary: Fix rounding and expiry-boundary bugs in a Spring Boot loyalty API, add FIFO redemption of expiring point lots and a paginated statement, then make redemptions concurrency-safe and idempotent.
overview:
You've joined the digital team at **Bean and Brew**, a coffee chain. This Spring Boot service runs the loyalty programme: the till reports each purchase, members earn points at a rate set by their tier (Bronze, Silver or Gold), and the app lets them spend points on rewards. Points are earned in **lots** that expire 12 months after the day they were earned.

The codebase is layered the usual way: `controller/` maps HTTP to service calls, `service/` holds the rules (`PointsService` for members, earning, expiry, redemptions and the statement; `PointsPolicy` for the earning and expiry rules; `RewardCatalog`), `repository/` keeps everything in memory, `dto/` has the request and response records with Bean Validation annotations, and `exception/` turns errors into one JSON shape in `ApiExceptionHandler`. Anything that depends on today's date reads an injectable `Clock`.

Start with `README.md`: it is the API contract, with the earning and expiry rules, the status codes and the error shape. Then read `PointsService`, `PointsPolicy` and `PointsLot`. The tests use MockMvc and a `MutableClock`, so they exercise the real controllers, validation and error handling on any date they choose.

phases.title: Extra points and points that live a day too long
phases.instructions:
Two reports came in from store managers.

> *"A Silver member paid **19.90** at the till and the app told them they earned **25 points**. Our loyalty terms say 1.25 points per unit, rounded down, so it should be 24. We see the same thing with Gold members: **3.99** gave 6 points instead of 5."*

> *"A customer earned points on 15 March last year and still saw them in the app on **15 March** this year, and managed to spend them. Points are meant to be gone on their 12-month birthday."*

The README is the contract: points for a purchase are rounded down per purchase, and a lot is no longer spendable **on** its expiry date (the last spendable day is the day before).

**Done when** every test in `Phase1Test` passes. Reproduce each report with a request (or a test) before you change anything.
hints: Both reports are about a boundary, not about missing data. For the first, work out by hand what 19.90 x 1.25 is and compare it with what the API says. For the second, pick the dates: earned 2025-03-15, looked at on 2026-03-14 and on 2026-03-15.

Look at `PointsPolicy.pointsFor`: which `RoundingMode` turns 24.875 into 25? Then look at `PointsLot.isExpiredOn`, which every balance, lot listing and expiry sweep goes through: what does `today.isAfter(expiresOn)` say when `today` equals `expiresOn`?
Use `RoundingMode.DOWN` for the points, and make `isExpiredOn` return `!today.isBefore(expiresOn)`: a lot is expired from its expiry date onward, so the last spendable day is the day before.
phases.answer:
**Root cause 1: rounding.** `PointsPolicy.pointsFor` used `setScale(0, RoundingMode.HALF_UP)`. 19.90 x 1.25 = 24.875 rounds up to 25 and 3.99 x 1.5 = 5.985 rounds up to 6. The documented rule is to round down per purchase.

**Fix:** `RoundingMode.DOWN` (the amounts are positive, so `FLOOR` is the same). Every purchase is rounded on its own; nothing is carried over.

**Root cause 2: the expiry boundary.** `PointsLot.isExpiredOn` returned `today.isAfter(expiresOn)`, which is false on the expiry date itself, so a lot lived one extra day: it was still in the balance, still listed and still spendable on its 12-month birthday, and the `EXPIRE` sweep ran a day late.

**Fix:** `return !today.isBefore(expiresOn);`. The balance, the lot list and the sweep all use this one method, so one change fixes all of them.

**Verify:** `Phase1Test` (it moves the `MutableClock` to the day before and the day of expiry), plus a manual request on both dates.

phases.title: Redemptions from the oldest lots, and a statement
phases.instructions:
Build the redemption feature and the statement. Both endpoints exist and answer `501` until you implement them in `PointsService`.

**1. `POST /members/{id}/redemptions`** with `{"rewardId", "quantity"?}` (implement `PointsService.redeem`):

- `201` with `{"id", "memberId", "rewardId", "quantity", "pointsSpent", "balance", "lots", "date"}`. `pointsSpent` is the reward cost times the quantity, `balance` is what the member has afterwards, and `lots` lists the lots it consumed as `{"lotId", "points", "expiresOn"}`.
- Spend the **oldest unexpired lots first** (soonest expiry): take a lot completely before the next one; the last lot may be partly spent. Lots that have expired are never spent and never count towards the balance.
- `409 insufficient_points` when the spendable balance is below the cost; nothing is spent and nothing is written to the statement.
- `404 reward_not_found` or `404 member_not_found` for unknown ids. The request body validation (`rewardId` required, `quantity` 1 to 10) already exists.
- Add a `REDEEM` statement entry (`points` = points spent, `balanceAfter`, the redemption id in `redemptionId`).

**2. `GET /members/{id}/statement?page=0&size=20`** (implement `PointsService.statement`): the member's `EARN`, `REDEEM` and `EXPIRE` entries, newest first, as `{"items", "page", "size", "totalItems", "totalPages"}`. `page` is 0-based and defaults to 0; `size` defaults to 20 and must be 1 to 100. A page past the end is `200` with no items. Bad paging is `422 validation_error` with the parameters in `fields` (report every bad parameter at once); an unknown member is `404`. Lots that have expired by today must already appear as `EXPIRE` entries.

**Done when** `Phase1Test` and `Phase2Test` pass.
hints: Keep the controller thin: the rules belong in `PointsService`. Start `redeem` with the lookups (member, then reward) so a 404 changes nothing, then call `expireDueLots` so expired lots are out of the way before you read the balance. `spendableLots(memberId)` already returns the unexpired lots with points left, soonest expiry first.

Compute the cost as `reward.points() * request.quantityOrOne()`, compare it with the sum of the spendable lots and throw `InsufficientPointsException` if it is higher. Then walk the lots: `take = Math.min(need, lot.getRemaining())`, reduce `remaining`, record a `Redemption.LotUse`, and stop when `need` reaches 0. Append one `REDEEM` entry with `ledger.nextRedemptionId()`.

For the statement, validate `page >= 0` and `1 <= size <= 100` into one `ValidationFailedException` (a map of fields), call `expireDueLots`, then copy the statement (oldest first) and read entries from the end: for `i` from `page*size` up to `min(total, page*size + size)`, take `all.get(total - 1 - i)`. `totalPages` is `ceil(total / size)`. Use a `long` for `page * size`.
phases.answer:
**Redemption:** look up the member and the reward (404 before anything changes), `expireDueLots` so expiry entries are written first, take `spendableLots` (already filtered and sorted by `expiresOn`), and check the sum against `reward.points() * quantity`; if it is lower, throw `InsufficientPointsException` (409). Otherwise consume lots in order with `take = min(need, remaining)`, building the `LotUse` list, and append one `REDEEM` entry whose `balanceAfter` is the old balance minus the cost. Cost O(lots) per redemption.

**Why oldest first:** it is the lot that expires soonest, so spending it first wastes the fewest points. Lots with the same expiry keep the order they were earned in because the sort is stable.

**Statement:** validate paging (both problems reported together), sweep expiry so `EXPIRE` entries exist for lots that expired since the last request, then page over the append-only statement newest first. O(size) per page after an O(n) copy. A page past the end is a normal `200` with no items.

Status codes follow the README: `201` for a redemption, `404` for unknown ids, `409` for a balance that is too low (the request is fine; the state of the member conflicts with it), `422` for anything the client fixes by changing the request.

phases.title: Parallel redemptions and safe retries
phases.instructions:
The till app retries a redemption when the network drops, and support has found customers charged twice. Load testing found something worse: when many redemptions for one member arrive together, the same points get spent more than once and the balance no longer matches the statement.

Make redemptions production-safe:

**1. Concurrency.** Redemptions, purchases and reads for one member running in parallel must never spend the same points twice, never take a lot (or the balance) below zero, and keep the statement consistent: the newest entry's `balanceAfter` equals the balance, and total earned minus total redeemed minus total expired equals the balance. A redemption that cannot be afforded is still `409`.

**2. Idempotency.** `POST /members/{id}/redemptions` accepts an optional `Idempotency-Key` header (1 to 64 letters, digits, `-` or `_`; anything else is `422 validation_error` with the header name in `fields`).

- A repeat of a successful request with the same key and the same body returns the original response again (`201`, the same `id`, and the same JSON) with the header `Idempotent-Replayed: true`, and spends nothing. A first execution sends `Idempotent-Replayed: false`.
- The same key with a different body (a different `rewardId` or `quantity`) is `422` with code `idempotency_key_reuse`.
- Only successes are remembered: if the first attempt failed (say `409 insufficient_points`), a retry with the same key runs again.
- This must hold when the retries arrive **at the same time**, from many threads.

**Done when** all three test classes pass. `Phase3Test` fires 30 parallel redemptions at ten lots, sends the same key from 16 threads, and mixes purchases and redemptions on 8 threads.
hints: There are two separate races. One is check-then-act on the lots: two threads both see 100 points left in the same lot, both pass the balance check and both spend it. The other is check-then-act on the key: two retries both see 'key not used yet' and both redeem.

For the lots, give each `Member` a `ReentrantLock` and hold it around everything that reads or changes that member's lots and statement: `earn`, `redeem`, `describe` and `statement` (the last two sweep expired lots, which writes). Different members then still run in parallel. For keys, claim the key atomically with `ConcurrentHashMap.putIfAbsent`, not `containsKey` followed by `put`.

Store a `CompletableFuture<Redemption>` plus a fingerprint of the request (reward id and quantity) under `memberId|key` with `putIfAbsent`. The winner runs the redemption and completes the future; everyone else compares fingerprints (422 `idempotency_key_reuse` if they differ) and `join()`s the future, which is a replay. If the winner fails, `remove(key, entry)` and complete the future exceptionally, so the key can be retried. Validate the header format in the controller and send `Idempotent-Replayed`.
phases.answer:
**Why phase 2 breaks.** `redeem` reads the lots, checks the sum, then decrements `remaining` with a plain read-modify-write. Two threads can read the same lot at once, both pass the check and both spend it: more redemptions succeed than the points allow, a lot is consumed twice, and a `REDEEM` entry's `balanceAfter` no longer matches the next one. The key race is the same pattern: without an atomic claim, 16 simultaneous retries are 16 redemptions.

**Locking.** Each `Member` holds a `ReentrantLock`, and `earn`, `redeem`, `describe` and `statement` run their whole read, check, write and append sequence inside it (even the reads, because they trigger the expiry sweep, which mutates lots and appends entries). The lock is per member, so unrelated members never wait for each other; a single global lock would also be correct but would serialize every redemption in the chain. There is no second lock to acquire, so there is no deadlock risk. Looking up the member and the reward happens outside the lock because it reads immutable data.

**Idempotency.** `IdempotencyStore` keeps `memberId|key -> (fingerprint, CompletableFuture<Redemption>)` in a `ConcurrentHashMap`. `putIfAbsent` makes exactly one request the owner of a key; the others wait for its future and replay the stored `Redemption` (so even `balance` is the original value), or get `422 idempotency_key_reuse` if their fingerprint differs. A failure releases the key with `remove(key, entry)`, so a `409` can be retried. The store holds the redemption outside the member lock, so a replay never waits on the lock. O(1) per request. In production the entries would expire (24 hours, say) and live in shared storage, such as a table with a unique constraint on the key, because the service runs on more than one instance.

**Verify:** `Phase3Test` checks the replay, the reuse, bad keys, a retry after a `409`, 16 concurrent retries producing one redemption, 30 parallel redemptions against 1000 points (exactly 10 succeed and every lot is spent exactly once), and the statement arithmetic after mixed parallel traffic.

debrief: Why did a purchase of 19.90 earn 25 points, and why did a lot survive its expiry date? How did you confirm each cause, and why was one change enough for the balance, the lot list and the expiry entries?
How does your redemption choose lots, and why oldest-expiry first? Where did you check for insufficient points so a 409 changes nothing, and what does one statement page cost?

What exactly could go wrong when 30 threads redeem against the same lots, and how does your lock prevent it without blocking other members? How do 16 simultaneous retries with one Idempotency-Key end up spending points once, and if an AI assistant wrote the locking code, how did you check it?
